Chapter 2: Discovering Purpose in Uniform
Sometimes, the next step in life sneaks up on you—almost like it’s waiting around the corner. For a young man fresh out of high school, college seemed like the obvious move. But honestly, it just didn’t light a fire inside. City College of New York had plenty of opportunity, sure, but those lectures and thick textbooks? They felt a million miles away from the big, urgent questions about what it means to grow up.
And then… there was the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps—ROTC. That’s where something finally clicked. The very first time he put on that uniform, the world just seemed to shift. Suddenly, there was order. There was belonging. He felt like he was part of something bigger than himself. The discipline of military life—crack-of-dawn mornings, sharp salutes, and the camaraderie that comes from working side by side—brought out strengths he never even knew he had.
The instructors? Most of them were veterans, and they became unexpected mentors. They didn’t just drill tactics and strategy—they showed what real leadership looked like. Integrity, quiet confidence, the kind of steadiness that comes from knowing where you fit in a team… these were lessons you could feel, not just hear.
For a young man from the Bronx, the military offered a whole new kind of meritocracy. In uniform, nobody cared where you came from or what your parents did. What mattered was how you carried yourself—how you treated others, and whether you could keep your cool under pressure. Those childhood lessons—respect, perseverance, staying humble—suddenly took on a whole new meaning, whether in the barracks or out on the drill field.
That’s not to say it was easy. The military had its own share of prejudice and tough moments. There were times when he felt overlooked, underestimated—like he was invisible in plain sight. But there were also these moments of unexpected kindness: a senior officer offering advice, a fellow cadet turning into a true friend, a team coming together just when it mattered most. These experiences showed him that leadership wasn’t about rank or title—it was about earning trust and leading by example.
Graduation brought his commission as a second lieutenant. That’s when responsibility really hit home. The Army was a world built on rules and routines, but it was also filled with people—soldiers from every walk of life, each with their own story, their own dreams and challenges. Leading them wasn’t just a duty; it was a privilege and a serious test. And he learned quickly: the best leaders don’t just talk—they listen. They care about their people, not just as soldiers, but as individuals.
Those early years in uniform? They were all about growth. Mistakes happened—orders came out too fast, decisions were rushed, and sometimes, pride got in the way of learning. But there were victories, too—big and small. A platoon that finally gelled as a team. A mission pulled off against the odds. Even a simple letter home that made a parent beam with pride.
Through it all, that sense of purpose only grew stronger. The military wasn’t just a job; it was a calling. Sure, it demanded sacrifice. But it also gave something back—meaning. In the discipline of service, in the bonds built through shared struggle, and in those quiet moments at the end of a long day, that young officer started to find the beginnings of a life’s work. The journey was just getting started, but the path ahead was finally starting to come into focus.
